title: Decidability of every level of the dot-depth hierarchy
formal: For every fixed integer k≥0, is there an algorithm that, given a deterministic finite automaton over a finite alphabet A, always halts and decides whether its language belongs to DD_k(A), the k-th dot-depth level defined below?
definitions: For each finite nonempty alphabet A, let A* be its finite words, ε the empty word, and A+=A*∖{ε}. Set DD₀(A)={∅,{ε},A+,A*}. For a class C of languages over A, Pol(C) consists of all finite unions of marked products L₀a₁L₁⋯a_rL_r, where r≥0, each a_i∈A, and every L_i∈C; r=0 gives L₀. Let Bool(C) be closure under finite union, finite intersection and complement relative to A*. Define DD_{k+1}(A)=Bool(Pol(DD_k(A))). The input automaton is given by finite explicit tables, including its alphabet, initial state and accepting states; its accepted language is L(M). The question quantifies ∀k∃a total Turing algorithm A_k∀M, with A_k(M)=yes exactly when L(M)∈DD_k(A). Each A_k must handle arbitrary finite input alphabets. No polynomial-time or elementary-time bound is requested. This fixes the full integer levels and the four-language level-zero convention; it does not merge distinct concatenation hierarchies or leave the logical signature implicit. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
context:
Finite automata provide a complete and effective representation of regular languages, but the number of states is only one measure of a language’s complexity. Another asks how complicated a logical description must be. Two automata with similar state counts can recognize languages requiring very different combinations of order, concatenation and negation. The dot-depth hierarchy measures that descriptive structure.

A marked product picks a sequence of distinguished letters and constrains the substrings around them. Over an alphabet containing a and b, A*aA*bA* says that some a occurs before some later b. Replacing the middle A* by {ε} requires the two distinguished letters to be adjacent. Boolean combinations can require several such patterns or forbid them. Iterating these operations permits the pieces between distinguished letters to satisfy properties that were already built at earlier levels.

The level is a minimum over all descriptions of the same language. Seeing four layers in a supplied expression does not prove the language needs four: another expression may be simpler. The input is therefore an automaton, rather than a proposed optimal expression. The algorithm must discover whether some description at the requested level exists, regardless of how the language was initially presented.

The union of the levels is the star-free class, whose membership is decidable through the aperiodicity of the syntactic monoid. This answers whether any finite level suffices, while the present question asks about a prescribed bound. Place and Zeitoun’s account of the dot-depth problem emphasizes this distinction between the classical star-free theorem and the finer unresolved classification.

There is a useful logical interpretation: full levels correspond to Boolean combinations of first-order formulas with bounded quantifier alternation, with the appropriate word predicates. The closely related Straubing–Thérien hierarchy starts from just the empty and universal languages and uses the order-only signature. Dot-depth also captures successor information. The card defines the language operations directly so that changing the basis or adding predicates cannot silently change its target.

Positive instances are effectively enumerable. Enumerate expressions at level k, convert each to a finite automaton, and check language equality with the input. If a suitable expression exists this eventually finds it. The obstruction is recognizing negative instances: continuing to search without success is not a certificate that every candidate fails. A decision theorem needs an effective stopping criterion or an equivalent finite characterization.

Separation and covering have supplied such information at lower levels. Separation asks whether a language from the chosen class can contain one given regular language while avoiding another. Covering generalizes this to a finite family of candidate covering languages and a finite list of languages they must avoid individually. Place and Zeitoun’s 2021 paper proves separation and covering for dot-depth two, giving information stronger than simple membership at that level.

Their 2024 result uses a generic algebraic characterization of Boolean polynomial closure. For levels at least two, it reduces membership at the next full level to covering at the preceding level. Together with the known covering result, this decides dot-depth three. The reduction does not by itself decide covering at every new level, so it cannot simply be iterated to settle the entire hierarchy.

A January 2025 preprint by Barloy, Cadilhac, Paperman and Straubing announced decidability of the first-order alternation hierarchy and related half-level results. It was withdrawn on January 31: the authors identify a fatal flaw in the proof of Lemma 19. The unchanged title and abstract still appear in search results, so they cannot be treated as an established resolution. No corrected replacement resolving this card was found in the present review.

Meanwhile, MeSCaL turns existing membership theorems into usable tests for many regular-language classes. Its second 2025 paper develops computations for level two and intermediate levels, and explicitly describes the general hierarchy problem as open. Lambert’s July 2026 work develops decompilation methods instantiated for dot-depth one and related extensions. These provide useful descriptions and implementations within known classes, without establishing decidability at every level.

Settling the question would determine whether a major logical complexity measure for regular languages can always be recognized effectively at any prescribed finite level. It would also clarify which finite algebraic information is sufficient to describe bounded alternation. An undecidable level would be equally revealing: even these finite-state languages would resist a complete algorithmic classification by that natural form of descriptive simplicity.
why: Determine whether bounded logical alternation can be recognized effectively throughout a fundamental hierarchy of regular languages.

importance.reason: A longstanding structural decision problem linking finite automata, logical definability and finite monoids; a full solution would explain much more than the known low-level algorithms.

progress.text: Generic concatenation-hierarchy methods organize membership, separation and covering and explain transfers between levels.
Place–Zeitoun establish separation and covering for dot-depth two.
Place–Zeitoun prove decidable membership at dot-depth three via a reduction to covering at the preceding level.
The announced full alternation-hierarchy theorem is withdrawn because of a fatal flaw in Lemma 19.
MeSCaL implements many established membership tests, including optimizations for level two and intermediate levels; the general problem remains explicit.
Lambert develops effective decompilation methods instantiated for dot-depth one and tier-based extensions, a restricted rather than all-level result.

status_note: No theorem deciding every fixed full dot-depth level was found through 11 September 2026. Full level three is decidable by Place–Zeitoun 2024. The January 2025 announced full alternation result remains explicitly withdrawn. This card fixes the four-language dot-depth basis, integer levels and per-fixed-level decidability; half levels and other bases are related questions.

sentences: The dot-depth hierarchy sorts star-free regular languages by how repeatedly concatenation and Boolean operations must be combined.
Given a finite automaton and a fixed level, the project asks whether membership in that level can always be decided.
The relevant level concerns the simplest possible description of the language, rather than the syntax initially supplied.
Deciding star-freeness only establishes membership somewhere in the hierarchy and does not identify a prescribed level.
An effective test for every level would connect automaton behavior to precise bounds on logical descriptive complexity.
